description:
We’re Zero-G Forge, a passionate team of makers and students from Private KOSBI Z.M.C. Technical High School, Turkey. We focus on zero-g systems, robotics, 3D CAD, rapid prototyping, and data. We are eager to turn NASA data into a real, impactful project.

Why join? We offer a highly collaborative, hands-on, and energetic environment where your ideas will shape the build.
summary:
"ZERO G FORCE" is an interactive, zero-server-load 3D web simulation built with Next.js and React Three Fiber. We transformed 13 historic NASA spacecraft—resting on the Moon, Mars, and in deep space—from cold hardware debris into relatable explorers that narrate their own missions in the first person using emotive AI voices.

Our project addresses the "Abandoned but not Forgotten" challenge by merging cinematic storytelling with physical-based rendering (PBR) and scientifically accurate data. Through our custom real-time Deep Space Network (DSN) telemetry panel, users can visually and mathematically simulate light-speed delays (RTLT) to truly grasp astronomical distances.

This project is important because it revitalizes invaluable space heritage for the Artemis Generation. By replacing dry statistics with empathy-driven narratives and experiential learning, it serves as a powerful educational tool that helps youth comprehend the colossal scale of the universe and the enduring legacy of human exploration.
details:
How it Works & What it Does "ZERO G FORCE" is an interactive 3D web simulation built with a Next.js and React Three Fiber architecture. The platform hosts 13 historic NASA spacecraft left on the Moon, Mars, and in deep space. When a user selects a spacecraft (e.g., Pioneer 10), the camera executes a cinematic transition to the 3D model. The spacecraft then begins to narrate its own mission story in the first person, using a character-specific AI voice generated by ElevenLabs. Simultaneously, our custom-coded "Deep Space Network (DSN) Telemetry Panel" appears, calculating and simulating the real-time distance and Round-Trip Light Time (RTLT) between Earth and the spacecraft using a custom light-speed engine.

Benefits & Intended Impact Our primary benefit is transforming cold, dry space statistics into empathetic, relatable narratives. For our target audience of 8-15 year olds, displaying billions of kilometers as a mere number is too abstract. However, realizing that "it takes 38 hours just to get a 'message received' signal back from this probe" allows them to viscerally grasp the colossal scale of the universe. The intended impact is to educate the Artemis Generation that these discarded machines are not "space junk," but eternal monuments of human exploration, fostering both a scientific and emotional connection.

Tools, Languages & Technologies Used To ensure a "Zero Server Load" architecture and smooth performance, we utilized a modern tech stack:

  • Framework & Language: Next.js 14, React, and TypeScript.
  • 3D Graphics Engine: React Three Fiber and Three.js (utilizing WebGL2 hardware acceleration).
  • Models & Materials: Original NASA .glb 3D models, enhanced with Physically Based Rendering (PBR) materials to realistically simulate Kapton gold foils and titanium surfaces reacting to cosmic light.
  • Styling & UI: Tailwind CSS, featuring VisionOS-style high-contrast backdrop blur filters.
  • Deployment: Vercel (Static Export architecture).

Project Creativity The creativity of our project lies in the seamless fusion of hard data visualization with cinematic storytelling. We didn't just place 3D models on a screen; we gave them a soul. We voiced the tiny Sojourner rover with the high-pitched excitement of a curious child, and the boundary-pushing Pioneer probe with the deep, philosophical tone of an old, brave captain. By doing so, we successfully bridged the gap between strict scientific data, digital art, and emotional storytelling.

Factors Our Team Considered

  • Scientific Validity: To ensure the DSN telemetry wasn't just a visual mock-up, we integrated a mathematical algorithm based on the exact speed of light constant (c = 299,792 km/s) to accurately calculate real-time communication delays.
  • Performance: To make the project accessible to students worldwide without requiring expensive servers, we optimized the application to run natively in the browser at a smooth 60 FPS using a Static Export architecture.
  • Global Accessibility: We designed the user interface and all character narratives entirely in English—the universal language of science and space exploration. This ensures that the simulation is seamlessly accessible, immersive, and perfectly understandable for a worldwide audience and the international judging panel.
